label: AQ 0024
title: The merge that swallowed the cursor

questions.q: Can't we just turn on token healing and ship?
questions.a: Not without measuring. Token healing, from the guidance library, backs up one token and forces the next token to start with the removed text. Xu et al. (2026) found it mixed: on code it lifted Qwen3-32B from 5.05% to 94.09%, but in German it stayed below the aligned score, and “it is not known in advance how far to back off”. An exact method they tested, ByteSampler, reached 100% on code for about one extra pass through the model.

questions.q: Bits per byte improved too. Do you approve then?
questions.a: Not on that alone. Bits per byte fixes the units, but it's still measured on whole files from the start, never at a cursor. In the SuperBPE study (COLM 2025), tiny bits-per-byte differences ranked its models differently from task scores. The deciding number is completion quality at real cursor positions.

teach.title: How it works: why the cursor suffers, and what to check

questions.q: Editors also send the code after the cursor. Does that matter?
questions.a: Yes. In fill-in-the-middle completion the file is cut twice at the cursor. Phan et al. (2024) note such prompts “may terminate mid-token”; their byte-level method gained 18% on fill-in-the-middle coding benchmarks and beat token healing. My reasoning: healing repairs where the prompt ends, not the cut text after the cursor.

teach.title: How it works: why the cursor suffers, and what to check

questions.q: Why can't you compare loss per token across two tokenizers?
questions.a: Bigger tokens carry more text each, so loss per token measures something different under each tokenizer. Bits per byte divides total surprise by the text's size in bytes, which is the same for both.

teach.title: How it works: why the cursor suffers, and what to check

questions.q: What did Xu et al. (2026) find when code prompts ended in the middle of a token?
questions.a: On 5,223 code prompts built to end mid-token, Qwen3-32B's output began with the true continuation 5.05% of the time, against 88.48% when each prompt was cut back to a token boundary. Larger models were equally or more affected.

questions.q: A 30-character line has 10 tokens, then 6 after free merging. At how many of its 29 inside positions can a cursor sit on a token edge, before and after?
questions.a: 9 before (one fewer than the tokens) and 5 after: about 31% falls to 17%, so most pause points land inside a token.
